summary: Psalm 82 pictures God presiding in the great assembly and judging figures called “gods” for unjust judgment. The poem moves from accusation, to commands to protect the vulnerable, to a warning that these exalted figures will die, and ends by asking God to judge the whole earth.
whyItMatters: Within Psalms, this chapter gives public voice to outrage over corrupt judgment and places every lesser authority under God’s rule. It also shows how short Hebrew poetry can use a courtroom scene to press a large claim about justice among the nations.

context.author: Associated in its heading with Asaph; Psalms is an anthology with headings whose exact force can include authorship, association, dedication, or collection.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping and instructed community, and later Jewish and Christian communities that received the Psalms for prayer and teaching.
context.date: The anthology includes poems from the monarchy through the postexilic period; this psalm names no date or specific historical occasion.
context.setting: Book III of the Psalms, where sanctuary, collapse, and failed rule are recurring concerns.
context.literaryForm: Compressed Hebrew poetry, here shaped as a scene of divine judgment with accusation, command, verdict, and plea.

outline.heading: God judges the assembly
outline.note: The psalm opens with God presiding and judging among the gods.

outline.heading: The charge of unjust rule
outline.note: The addressed figures are accused of unjust judgment and partiality toward the wicked.

outline.heading: The duty of protection
outline.note: They are commanded to defend, maintain, rescue, and deliver the weak, poor, fatherless, needy, and oppressed.

outline.heading: Darkness and shaken foundations
outline.note: The poem describes ignorance, lack of understanding, wandering in darkness, and a world whose foundations are shaken.

outline.heading: Exalted status and mortal end
outline.note: Those called gods and sons of the Most High are told they will die like men and fall like rulers.

outline.heading: Appeal for God to judge the earth
outline.note: The closing prayer asks God to arise and judge, because all nations belong to him.

keyVerses.text: A Psalm by Asaph. God presides in the great assembly. He judges among the gods.
keyVerses.why: This verse frames the whole poem as a judgment scene, with God evaluating other exalted figures.

keyVerses.text: “Defend the weak, the poor, and the fatherless. Maintain the rights of the poor and oppressed.
keyVerses.why: This gives the clearest positive standard for the rulers or judges being addressed: justice is measured by protection of vulnerable people.

keyVerses.text: Nevertheless you shall die like men, and fall like one of the rulers.”
keyVerses.why: The warning overturns their elevated status by pronouncing that they will die.

keyVerses.text: Arise, God, judge the earth, for you inherit all of the nations.
keyVerses.why: The final line widens the scene from the assembly to the earth and all nations.

themes: defense of the weak and poor

questions.question: Who is speaking in this psalm?
questions.answer: The poem begins by describing God in a judging role, then presents direct speech accusing and warning the addressed figures. The final verse turns into a plea addressed to God: “Arise, God, judge the earth.” The chapter does not identify a human speaker beyond the heading’s association with Asaph.

questions.question: Who are the “gods” in verse 1?
questions.answer: Readers differ. Some understand the “gods” as heavenly beings in a divine council; others understand the word as a poetic or legal way of referring to human rulers or judges who exercise authority. The chapter itself shows that these figures are judged for injustice and told they will die like men, but it does not pause to define the term.

questions.question: What does the psalm say these judges are doing wrong?
questions.answer: They are accused of judging unjustly and showing partiality to the wicked. The next lines imply the opposite of their failure: they should defend the weak, maintain rights, rescue the needy, and deliver them from the wicked.

questions.question: Does this chapter treat poverty as guilt or failure?
questions.answer: No. The poor, weak, fatherless, needy, and oppressed are presented as people who should be defended and rescued. The moral criticism falls on those who judge unjustly and favor the wicked.

questions.question: What is “Selah”?
questions.answer: “Selah” appears at the end of verse 2. It is an uncertain musical or performance marker often preserved in translation because its exact instruction is no longer known. Here it is placed after the charge of unjust judgment and partiality.

questions.question: What does verse 5 mean by the foundations of the earth being shaken?
questions.answer: The verse links ignorance and darkness with cosmic-sounding instability: “All the foundations of the earth are shaken.” In the poem’s movement, corrupt judgment is not a small private defect; it threatens the ordered world the judges were supposed to uphold. The line is poetic, and the text does not require turning it into a physical description of the planet.

questions.question: Why say “You are gods” and then “you shall die like men”?
questions.answer: The contrast is the point of the warning. Whatever exalted title or role they have, they are not beyond judgment. Verse 7 brings them down to mortality: they will die and fall like rulers.

questions.question: How does the final verse change the scope of the psalm?
questions.answer: The final verse no longer addresses the unjust figures directly. It asks God to judge the earth and grounds that request in God’s inheritance of all nations. The poem moves from a scene within the “great assembly” to a claim about worldwide judgment.

questions.question: Is this psalm giving a full political program?
questions.answer: No. It gives a sharp poetic standard for judgment: do not favor the wicked, and protect the weak, poor, fatherless, needy, and oppressed. Applying that across times and systems requires care, because the chapter is an ancient poem and prayer, not a modern policy manual.

glossary.def: The name in the heading: “A Psalm by Asaph.” Such headings can indicate authorship, association, dedication, or belonging, and their exact historical force is debated.
The setting named in verse 1, where God presides and judges. The phrase helps create the chapter’s courtroom-like scene.

The figures among whom God judges in verse 1 and whom he addresses in verse 6. Readers differ on whether the term refers to heavenly beings, human rulers or judges, or a poetic overlap of authority language.
A preserved performance term in verse 2 whose exact meaning is uncertain.
A vulnerable group named in verse 3 alongside the weak and poor, whose rights the addressed judges are commanded to maintain.
